narrative:
Your application was reviewed by a predictive model that assessed your likelihood of passing the bar exam on the first attempt, and the model estimated a 51.8% probability that you would not pass — a result that sits right on the edge of the decision boundary, meaning your situation is genuinely close to the threshold for approval. Because the model predicted you would fail, your application was unfortunately rejected. It's important to understand that this decision was based on academic and background factors, and notably, your gender and racial background played no role in the model's assessment.

To help explain what drove this outcome, it's useful to think about "what if" scenarios — alternative versions of your profile that would have been enough to flip the prediction from "fail" to "pass." These scenarios don't describe what you must do in real life, but they reveal which factors the model considers most sensitive and where small changes could make a meaningful difference.

The model generated three such alternative scenarios, and the pattern across all three is remarkably consistent: in every single case, only one factor changed — your undergraduate GPA. No other feature, including your LSAT score, your law school grades, your family income, or your enrollment status, was altered in any of the three scenarios. This tells you clearly that, in the model's view, your undergraduate GPA is the single most influential lever in your profile right now.

The change required is also quite specific: across all three scenarios, your undergraduate GPA would need to decrease slightly, by an average of 0.2 points, from your current 3.40 to approximately 3.20. Interestingly, students who passed the bar exam had an average undergraduate GPA of 3.24, which means a GPA of 3.20 actually aligns more closely with the typical profile of a successful bar exam candidate in this dataset. This may seem counterintuitive — that a slightly lower GPA would help — but it reflects the complex, non-linear patterns the model has learned from historical data, where the combination of your specific scores and grades together shapes the prediction.

What this also means is that your other characteristics are not the problem. Your LSAT score of 36 is close to the average of 37.27 among students who passed, your full-time enrollment status matches 93% of students who successfully passed, and while your family income falls in the lower-middle bracket — a less common background among those who passed — it was not a factor the model needed to change in any scenario. Your law school grades in Years 1 and 3 also remained unchanged across all counterfactuals, suggesting the model does not see those as the primary barrier, even though they are currently well below the averages of students who passed.

The most actionable takeaway is that your profile is genuinely borderline, and the model's sensitivity to your undergraduate GPA — even by a small margin — suggests that how your overall academic record is contextualized and presented may matter. Since you cannot change your past GPA, this insight is most useful as a signal that strengthening other parts of your application, such as demonstrating strong preparation for the bar exam itself, could help shift the outcome in your favor.
